chunks: "In a buck the input current isn't smooth.
The high-side FET is only on for a fraction of the cycle, so the input current is a train of pulses, up to the inductor's peak current, say 1. 5 to 2. 5 amps in my 12 volts to 3.
3 volts, 2 amps example, with an average of only 0. 55 amps.
The supply and the cable feeding the converter have inductance and resistance, so they can't deliver those pulses with fast edges.
The input capacitor sits right at the FET and acts as a local reservoir: it supplies the pulses during the on time and gets recharged by the source at a nearly steady 0.
55 amps during the off time. If you remove it, the pulses would have to come through the cable inductance. A 1 microhenries cable and a current step of 1.

5 amps in 10 nanoseconds wants 150 volts, so the voltage at the FET collapses at turn-on, and at turn-off the cable current has to stop abruptly, so it rings or spikes with V equals I square root of L over C , easily over the FET rating.
You'd also have massive conducted EMI and a supply that droops or oscillates, and the controller could hit under-voltage lockout.
So the cap needs a low ESR and ESL, to be placed right at the high-side FET drain and low-side source, rated for the rms ripple current of about 0.
9 amps here, and sized so the input ripple is something like 50 to 100 millivolts."
